transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I came in because I’m losing a lot of time to things that probably sound small, but they don’t feel small when I’m stuck in them. I keep re-reading emails and texts over and over, reopening folders on my computer to check what’s in them, and before I leave the house or even just start work, I’ll mentally replay conversations or things I wrote, trying to make sure I didn’t miss something or make some serious mistake.

It’s not just a quick double-check. It can eat up these chunks of time, and I’ll think, “Okay, one more time and then I’ll move on,” but then I’m not satisfied, so I do it again. It’s like I’m trying to prove to myself that everything is fine, but I never quite get that proof. It’s gotten frustrating enough that I figured I should talk to someone about it.
Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yes. That’s actually one of the main things that’s bothering me. It’s not like I’m sitting there trying to think about it — it barges in when I’m doing something completely different.

Like, I’ll be trying to work through a system design problem, or prepare a lesson, and suddenly this thought pops up that maybe I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or maybe I mishandled some family photos somehow, or that I’ve let someone in the community down. And then I’ll try to tell myself, “No, you already went through this, you already checked this, it’s probably fine,” but it doesn’t really settle.

It’s hard to explain, because the thought doesn’t always feel logical, but it feels urgent. Like if I don’t address it, I’m being careless or irresponsible. So even when I know I’ve gone over it already, my mind keeps circling back to it, and it interrupts whatever I’m supposed to be doing.
Do you experience any physical sensations, like tension or restlessness, when these repeating thoughts occur?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I haven’t really been paying attention to my body in those moments as much as what’s going on in my head.

I mean, I can tell I feel keyed up in some way, but if you asked me, “Is it tension in your shoulders?” or “Do you feel restless?” I don’t know that I could say clearly. It’s more that my attention gets sort of locked onto the thought, and I’m trying to resolve it mentally. I may be tense, but I haven’t really tracked it that specifically.

So… I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure. I notice the mental pressure much more than any physical sensation.
Do you ever avoid certain activities or situations because of these repeating thoughts or the need to check things?

Yes… I mean, maybe not avoid in the obvious sense, like refusing to go somewhere, but it has definitely changed what I take on and how I show up.

At work, it slows me down a lot. I’m in a computer-related job, and there are design milestones I’m supposed to hit, and I’ve missed some because I get stuck checking or re-reading or going back through things before I can move forward. It’s embarrassing because I used to be pretty reliable about that kind of thing. And I’ve had to postpone mentoring sessions I normally would handle without much trouble, because I wasn’t ready or I’d lost too much time trying to make sure everything was correct.

There was also this youth coding workshop that mattered to me — I really wanted to do a good job with it — and I ended up late and not as prepared as I should have been. I felt really embarrassed about that. It wasn’t that I didn’t care. If anything, I cared too much and got tangled up trying to make sure I hadn’t missed anything. So yes, I guess I do avoid or delay things sometimes, or I end up not doing them the way I intended, because the checking takes over.
Do you feel like you have to perform certain actions or rituals in a specific way to reduce your anxiety or discomfort?

Yes, I think so. I don’t know if I’d call them rituals exactly, because that sounds so formal, but there are definitely things I feel like I have to do before I can move on.

A big part of why I came in is that I keep losing these big chunks of time re-reading emails and texts. Not just proofreading once, but going back again and again, checking the wording, checking whether I might have sent it to the wrong person, or whether something could be misunderstood. And then I’ll reopen folders on my computer to make sure a file is where I think it is, or that I didn’t delete or move something important. Sometimes I know I just looked, but it doesn’t “stick,” if that makes sense.

And before I leave the house or before I start work, I can get caught mentally replaying conversations — like, “Did I say something wrong? Did I imply something I didn’t mean? Did I forget to do something I agreed to?” It feels like I’m trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. I’ll go over it from different angles, almost like I’m building a case in my head, but it still doesn’t feel settled for very long.

So yes, there’s this pressure to do the checking or the replaying in a certain way until it feels safe enough to continue, though it often takes much longer than I intend.
Have you noticed any impact on your relationships with family or friends due to these habits of checking and replaying conversations?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I haven’t noticed a clear, direct effect on my relationships in the way I notice it with work or tasks.

I mean, I do replay conversations with people, including family or friends sometimes, but I don’t know that anyone has specifically said, “You’re doing this and it’s affecting me,” or anything like that. It’s more internal, at least from what I can tell. I might spend time afterward going over what I said or wondering if something came across wrong, but I can’t say for sure that it has changed the relationship itself.

Maybe there are small things I’m not fully aware of — like maybe I’m distracted or slower to respond sometimes — but I wouldn’t want to say it’s definitely caused problems if I don’t know that. So I guess my answer is: I haven’t really noticed a major impact, but I may not be the best judge of it.
Are there any areas of your life, besides work, where you feel like these habits of checking and replaying are causing you a lot of distress or problems?

Besides work… I think the clearest other example is that youth coding workshop I mentioned. I know that’s still kind of computer-related, but it wasn’t my regular job. It was more personal, something I cared about doing well, and I ended up late and not prepared the way I should have been because I lost so much time checking things and trying to make sure everything was right.

That one bothered me a lot, honestly. I felt embarrassed, because it wasn’t that I was being careless. It was almost the opposite — I was trying so hard not to make a mistake that I made the whole thing worse. And with mentoring sessions too, even though some of that connects to work, those feel more personal to me because I used to be someone people could count on for that. Now I’ve had to postpone them when I get behind or when I’m not ready because I’ve spent too long checking and rechecking.

So yes, outside of just my day-to-day work tasks, it causes distress when it gets in the way of commitments I care about, especially when other people are expecting me to show up prepared.
Are there any personal relationships or social activities that you feel are being negatively affected by your need to check and replay things?

Socially… I don’t know if I’d say friendships have clearly suffered, like I haven’t had a big falling-out or anything like that. But the places where other people are depending on me, yes, that’s where it shows up.

Work has definitely slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that spills into things that feel more personal too. I used to be pretty reliable with mentoring sessions, and now I’ve had to postpone some of them because I wasn’t ready or I got stuck checking and rechecking things. That bothers me more than I expected, because mentoring is something I actually care about, not just another task on a list.

And there was that youth coding workshop… I was late and not really prepared the way I should have been. I felt really embarrassed about that. It mattered to me, and I wanted to do a good job, but I lost so much time trying to make sure everything was right that I ended up letting people down anyway. So, yes, maybe not in my close personal relationships exactly, but social or community commitments — yes, those have been affected.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is interfering with your overall quality of life?

Yes… I think it is. I don’t want to overstate it like everything in my life has fallen apart, because it hasn’t, but my overall quality of life is definitely worse than it used to be.

The biggest thing is that I don’t feel reliable in the same way anymore. My work has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that’s not like me. I used to be able to move through things, check them reasonably, and then let them go. Now I can lose so much time going back over things that I end up behind anyway, even though the whole point was to avoid making a mistake.

And it doesn’t just stay at work. I’ve had to postpone mentoring sessions I used to handle pretty reliably, and that bothers me because those are things I care about. They’re not just obligations — I feel like people are expecting me to show up prepared, and I used to be able to do that.

The youth coding workshop was probably the one that really made me feel embarrassed. I was late and not prepared the way I wanted to be, and it mattered to me. I wanted to do a good job for them. So yes, when I look at it that way, it is interfering with my quality of life — not every minute of every day, but enough that I feel disappointed in myself and like I’m not functioning at the level I should be.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is causing you significant distress or interfering with your ability to function in your daily life?

Yes, I do. I mean, I keep wanting to say it’s not catastrophic, because I’m still getting through the day, but it’s definitely interfering more than I’m comfortable admitting.

At work, it’s slowed me down enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that really bothers me because I used to be someone who could keep pace and be dependable. Now I can get stuck checking or replaying things to the point where the time just disappears, and then I’m behind anyway.

And it’s not just regular work tasks. I’ve had to postpone mentoring sessions that I used to handle pretty reliably, and that feels personal to me. Those are people expecting me to be prepared and present, and I hate feeling like I’m letting them down.

The youth coding workshop was probably the clearest example outside my normal routine. I was late and not prepared the way I wanted to be, and I was honestly embarrassed. It mattered to me, and I wanted to do it well, but I lost so much time trying to make sure everything was right that I ended up not functioning well when it counted. So yes — it causes distress, and it is affecting my daily life in a real way.
Do you feel compelled to repeat certain mental actions, like counting or repeating specific words, as part of your checking or replaying thoughts?

Not exactly counting, no. I don’t really have a specific word or number I repeat, at least not that I’ve noticed.

It’s more like… I get pulled into repeating the review itself. I’ll re-read an email or a text over and over, not because I enjoy it or because I’m still editing it in a useful way, but because I’m trying to feel certain I didn’t say something wrong or miss something serious. Or I’ll reopen a folder I already checked, sometimes more than once, just to prove to myself the file is really there or that I didn’t overlook something.

And with conversations, it’s not a phrase I repeat so much as mentally replaying the whole exchange. Before I leave the house or before I start work, I can get stuck going back through what I said, what they said, whether I implied the wrong thing, whether I forgot something important. It feels like I’m trying to settle the question in my mind, like, “Okay, there wasn’t a serious mistake,” but it doesn’t stay settled for very long.

So no, not counting or special words, but yes, there’s definitely a repetitive mental checking part to it.
Are there any situations or activities that you avoid entirely because of your need to check and replay things?

I’m not sure I’d say I avoid anything entirely. At least, nothing comes to mind where I think, “I just can’t do that anymore, so I don’t.” It’s more… I may hesitate, or I may take longer to get myself started, because I know I can get caught in checking afterward or before I do it.

But avoid entirely? I don’t think so. I still do the basic things I need to do. I might dread certain things a bit more, especially if they involve sending something out or being responsible for details, but I haven’t completely stopped doing them.

I guess the honest answer is that I haven’t really noticed full avoidance as much as getting slowed down or stuck once I’m in the activity. So, no — not entirely, not that I can identify.
Do you think these repeating thoughts and checking behaviors are reasonable and justified, or do you see them as excessive or irrational?

I see them as excessive, yes. I mean, in the moment they feel justified — that’s the tricky part. If I’m re-reading an email or a text, part of me is thinking, “Well, this is sensible, you’re just making sure you didn’t say something wrong.” Or if I reopen a folder, I tell myself I’m just confirming the file is really there and I didn’t miss it.

But then I’ll realize I’ve done it again and again, and I’m not actually finding anything new. I’m just trying to get this feeling of certainty, like I’m trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. And that’s when it starts to feel irrational, or at least out of proportion.

The same thing happens with conversations. Before I leave the house or start work, I can get stuck mentally replaying what was said, almost like I’m reviewing evidence. At first it seems reasonable, but after a while I know I’m not solving anything — I’m just losing chunks of time. So yes, I do recognize it’s excessive. I just don’t always feel that clearly when I’m in the middle of it.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your personal or professional relationships due to your need to check and replay things?

Yes, especially professionally. I wouldn’t say it’s destroyed relationships or anything that dramatic, but it has definitely affected how reliable I feel I am with people.

At work, my pace has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones. That’s hard for me to say, because I’ve always thought of myself as someone who could be counted on technically, and also someone who could help keep things moving. But the checking and re-checking eats into the time I should be using to actually make progress. So then I’m behind, and that affects other people waiting on my part.

I’ve also had to postpone mentoring sessions I used to handle pretty reliably. Those are important to me — I don’t like feeling like I’m letting people down, especially when someone is expecting guidance from me. It’s not that I don’t care or that I’m blowing it off. It’s more that I get bogged down trying to make sure everything is correct or that I haven’t missed something, and then I’m not ready when I should be.

And outside of work, there was a youth coding workshop that mattered to me, and I ended up being late and unprepared. I felt really embarrassed by that. It stuck with me because it wasn’t just some minor errand; it was something I wanted to show up well for. I don’t know if I’d call that a relationship problem exactly, but it definitely affected how I felt around the people involved, like I had failed them or looked careless when that wasn’t what was going on.
Are there any activities or tasks that you used to enjoy or feel comfortable doing, but now avoid because of your need to check and replay things?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if “avoid” is always the perfect word, because sometimes I still technically do the thing, but I delay it or I back away from it enough that the result is almost the same.

Work is the biggest example. I used to feel pretty comfortable moving through design tasks and getting things to a point where other people could build on them. I wouldn’t say I was careless before, but I could make decisions, check them once or twice, and move forward. Now I get slowed down so much by checking and replaying details that I’ve actually missed design milestones. And that’s not something that used to happen much, so it’s been really frustrating and honestly kind of embarrassing.

Mentoring is another one. I used to handle mentoring sessions pretty reliably, and I liked doing them. I felt useful in that role. But lately I’ve had to postpone some because I wasn’t ready or I got too bogged down trying to make sure I had everything right. So it’s not that I stopped caring about it — if anything, I care a lot — but I start feeling this pressure that I’m not prepared enough or I might miss something, and then I put it off.

And there was a youth coding workshop that mattered to me. I wanted to show up well for it, and I ended up late and unprepared. That one really stuck with me because it was something I would normally have felt good about doing. Instead I felt embarrassed, like I’d let people down or looked disorganized. So yes, I guess there are things I used to enjoy or feel competent doing that I now sort of dread or delay because I know I can get trapped in all the checking and replaying.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is affecting your ability to form or maintain close relationships?

I think it affects them indirectly more than directly, if that makes sense. I’m not sure I’d say I have trouble forming close relationships because of it, exactly, but maintaining the roles and commitments that matter to me has definitely gotten harder.

At work, for example, my checking and replaying things has slowed me down enough that I’ve missed design milestones. And that changes how I feel with people — I start worrying they see me as unreliable, or like I’m not pulling my weight. I’ve also had to postpone mentoring sessions that I used to handle pretty dependably, and those relationships matter to me. I don’t like having to tell someone I’m not ready or push them off, especially when I used to be the person who could show up and help.

And then there was a youth coding workshop that I really cared about. I ended up late and unprepared, and I was embarrassed by that. It wasn’t just being late — it was the feeling that people were counting on me and I didn’t come through. So, yes, I think it can interfere with maintaining closeness or trust, even if it’s not like I’m arguing with people or cutting them off. It’s more that I become less available, less dependable, and then I feel ashamed and pull back a bit.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is making it hard for you to enjoy social activities or spend time with friends and family?

Yes, I think it is, though maybe more through commitments than casual socializing. I keep coming back to this feeling that I’m not as available or dependable as I used to be.

The clearest example is work-related, but it spills over into how I feel around people. My work has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that’s not just a private problem — other people are waiting on me. Then I’m carrying this embarrassment or pressure into interactions, like I’m already behind before I even start talking to anyone.

I’ve also had to postpone mentoring sessions that I used to handle pretty reliably. Those were interactions I actually valued. I liked being able to sit with someone and help them think through a problem. But when I get caught up in checking and replaying whether I’ve prepared enough or whether something is right, I end up delaying, and then it stops feeling enjoyable. It becomes another situation where I’m afraid I’m letting someone down.

And the youth coding workshop is probably the closest example to what you’re asking. That mattered to me, and I wanted to show up well. Instead I was late and unprepared, and I felt really embarrassed. So afterward, instead of feeling connected or glad I participated, I was stuck thinking about how I must have looked careless or disorganized. That makes it harder to enjoy those kinds of activities, even when I genuinely want to be there.
Do you feel like these repeating thoughts are completely under your control, or do they sometimes occur against your will?

They definitely happen against my will. I mean, I wish they were more under my control, because if they were, I would just decide to stop and move on. But it doesn’t feel like that.

Even when I’m trying to focus on something totally different, like working through a system design or preparing a lesson, the thought will just barge in. It’ll be something like, “What if I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife?” or “What if I mishandled those family photos?” or “What if I let someone in the community down and I’m not really facing it?” And it’s not like I sit down and choose to think about those things. They just show up, and then once they’re there, it’s very hard to let them pass.

The frustrating part is that I often know I’ve already gone over it. I’ll think, “You already checked this, you already replayed it, there isn’t anything new here.” But that doesn’t make it feel settled. It’s like some part of my mind keeps insisting there’s still something unresolved, and if I don’t keep looking at it, I might miss something important. So no, I wouldn’t say they’re completely under my control. Sometimes they feel like they interrupt whatever I’m trying to do, and then I lose time trying to get back to where I was.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is significantly interfering with your ability to function socially or at work?

Yes. I think at this point I have to say it is interfering, especially at work. I’ve been trying not to make it sound bigger than it is, but the practical effect is pretty clear.

My work has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that’s not really something I can explain away as just being careful or thorough. Other people are depending on those pieces being done, and when I get caught checking and replaying things, I lose time and then I’m not where I should be. That affects how I function day to day, and honestly it affects how I see myself at work too.

I’ve also had to postpone mentoring sessions that I used to handle pretty reliably. That bothers me a lot, because those weren’t just random meetings — I cared about showing up for people in that way. I used to be able to prepare, meet with someone, and be helpful. Now it can turn into this whole process where I’m not ready, or I keep going back over whether I’ve prepared enough, and then I delay it. So socially or professionally, it makes me less dependable than I want to be.

And then there was the youth coding workshop, which still makes me feel embarrassed when I think about it. I was late and unprepared for something that mattered to me. I wanted to be useful there, and instead I felt like I showed up in this disorganized way. So yes, I’d say it’s significant — not that I can’t function at all, but it’s definitely getting in the way of work and the kinds of social or community roles I value.
Do you feel like your need to check and replay things is causing you significant distress or impairment in your daily life?

Yes, I would say it’s causing real impairment. I don’t always like admitting that, because part of me wants to frame it as, you know, I’m just being careful or I’m trying to be responsible. But the day-to-day consequences are harder to ignore now.

At work, my pace has slowed enough that I’ve missed design milestones, and that’s not a small thing in my line of work. Those milestones affect other people and their timelines, so when I get stuck checking or replaying things, it doesn’t just stay in my head. It turns into missed deadlines, delays, and this feeling that I’m becoming less reliable than I used to be.

I’ve also had to postpone mentoring sessions that I normally would have handled without much trouble. I used to be pretty dependable with those, and I actually liked doing them. But lately, if I’m caught up in whether I’m prepared enough or whether I’ve overlooked something, I end up pushing them back. That bothers me because those sessions mattered to me, and I don’t like feeling like I’m letting people down.

And socially, or maybe more in terms of community involvement, there was a youth coding workshop that I cared about. I was late and unprepared, and I felt really embarrassed afterward. It stuck with me because I wanted to show up well, and instead I felt disorganized and kind of ashamed. So yes, it’s distressing, and it’s impairing my daily life in ways I can’t really brush off anymore.
